actions.name: Review CT chest report (current)
actions.result: CT chest without contrast: Healing right lateral 7th rib fracture with mild callus formation, consistent with recent trauma. Incidental 7 mm solid pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe, non-calcified, smooth margins. Mild centrilobular emphysema. Bilateral calcified pleural plaques, most pronounced along the diaphragmatic and posterolateral pleura. No pleural effusion. No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. No prior chest CT available for comparison.

actions.name: Search prior imaging in regional exchange
actions.result: No prior CT, chest x-ray, or cross-sectional imaging found in this health system or regional image exchange network. This appears to be the patient's first chest CT.

actions.name: Apply Fleischner Society guidelines to nodule size/risk
actions.result: For a solid, single pulmonary nodule 6-8 mm in a high-risk patient (smoking history, occupational exposure), Fleischner 2017 guidance recommends CT follow-up at 6-12 months, then consider repeat at 18-24 months depending on findings, rather than immediate biopsy or PET.

actions.name: Review rib fracture healing status
actions.result: Right 7th rib fracture shows callus formation and bridging, consistent with a fracture roughly 4-6 weeks old and progressing through normal healing; no displacement or non-union.

actions.name: Review smoking history documented in chart
actions.result: Documented: 35 pack-years, quit 6 years ago at approximately age 57.

actions.name: Review occupational exposure history in chart
actions.result: Chart notes prior employment as a shipyard pipefitter with reported asbestos lagging exposure in the 1980s.

actions.name: Assess lung cancer screening eligibility (USPSTF criteria)
actions.result: Patient meets USPSTF criteria for annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening: age 50-80, 20+ pack-year smoking history, and current smoker or quit within the past 15 years. He has 35 pack-years and quit 6 years ago, so he remains within the eligibility window. He has not previously undergone a dedicated screening LDCT; this diagnostic CT was done for trauma, not screening.

actions.name: Determine whether findings suggest asbestos-related pleural disease vs malignant process
actions.result: Calcified pleural plaques are a benign marker of past asbestos exposure, not malignancy. They do not themselves require biopsy or oncologic workup, though they confirm exposure history and support ongoing surveillance by primary care/pulmonology.

actions.name: Compare nodule location/characteristics for suspicious features
actions.result: Nodule is solid with smooth, well-defined margins; no spiculation, no cavitation, no associated lymphadenopathy. These are reassuring but not definitive features; size and growth over time remain the key determinants per Fleischner guidance.

actions.name: Check home oxygen saturation reading if available
actions.result: Patient reports home pulse oximeter reading of 96% on room air today, no device photo available.

actions.name: Review emphysema severity on CT relative to symptoms
actions.result: Mild centrilobular emphysema noted on CT; no bullae, no evidence of severe airflow disease on this study. Correlate clinically with pulmonary function if indicated by referring provider.

actions.name: Confirm referring provider and next steps already documented
actions.result: Referring clinician (orthopedic urgent care) has been sent the full report; no biopsy, PET, or pulmonology referral has yet been placed. Radiology report impression recommends follow-up per Fleischner and correlation with smoking/occupational history.

actions.name: Review rib pain management plan from referring note
actions.result: Referring urgent care note from the fall visit recommends supportive care for rib fracture: activity as tolerated, ice, incentive spirometry to prevent pneumonia, and ibuprofen or acetaminophen for pain; no opioids prescribed.

artifacts.title: CT Chest Without Contrast - Final Report
artifacts.author: Radiology, Maine Coast Medical Imaging
artifacts.body:
CLINICAL HISTORY: 63-year-old male, fall with right-sided chest pain, rule out rib fracture.

TECHNIQUE: Non-contrast CT of the chest.

FINDINGS:
Bones: Healing fracture of the right lateral 7th rib with early callus formation, no displacement.
Lungs: 7 mm solid, smooth-margined, non-calcified nodule in the right upper lobe. Mild centrilobular emphysema. No other nodules, masses, or consolidation.
Pleura: Bilateral calcified pleural plaques along diaphragmatic and posterolateral surfaces, consistent with prior asbestos exposure. No effusion or pneumothorax.
Mediastinum/Hila: No lymphadenopathy. Heart size normal.
Upper abdomen (limited): Unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:
1. Healing right 7th rib fracture, consistent with reported trauma.
2. Incidental 7 mm solid right upper lobe pulmonary nodule - recommend follow-up CT per Fleischner Society guidelines given smoking and occupational exposure history (6-12 months, then consider 18-24 months).
3. Calcified pleural plaques bilaterally, consistent with prior asbestos exposure; benign finding.
4. Mild emphysema.

artifacts.title: Urgent Care Visit Note - Fall/Rib Injury
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Lindqvist, Urgent Care
artifacts.body: 63-year-old male presents after slipping on ice 1 day prior, landing on right side. Point tenderness over right lateral ribs, worse with deep breath. No shortness of breath, no hemoptysis, no fever. CT chest ordered to evaluate for fracture. Plan: supportive care, ice, incentive spirometry, OTC analgesia, follow up with primary care in 1-2 weeks and discuss incidental CT findings. Advised against opioids given minimal benefit and fall risk.

facts.chart: Patient called after reading 'nodule' in his CT portal result and wants to know if it is cancer.
facts.says: I read my own scan report online before anyone called me. It says 'nodule' in my lung. Just tell me straight - do I have cancer?

facts.chart: Fell on ice two days ago, landed on right side, right-sided chest wall pain prompted the CT.
facts.says: I slipped on some ice outside my house and came down hard on my right side. That's why they scanned my chest, for the ribs.

facts.chart: Patient reports not sleeping since viewing report online.
facts.says: I haven't slept right in two nights since I saw that word on the screen.

facts.chart: Denies shortness of breath, cough, or hemoptysis.
facts.says: No, I'm not coughing anything up and I'm not more short of breath than usual.

facts.chart: Pain is localized to the right rib area, worse with deep breath or coughing, improved with acetaminophen.
facts.says: It hurts right where I landed, mostly when I take a deep breath or cough. The Tylenol helps some.

facts.chart: Denies unintentional weight loss.
facts.says: My weight's been the same, nothing's changed there.

facts.chart: Denies appetite changes.
facts.says: Eating fine, no issues there.

facts.chart: Denies fever, chills, or night sweats.
facts.says: No fevers, no sweating through the sheets or anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports feeling tired but attributes it to poor sleep since seeing the report, not a new baseline symptom.
facts.says: I'm wiped out, but that's from not sleeping, not from before.

facts.chart: Smoked 1 pack per day for 35 years, quit 6 years ago.
facts.says: Aye, I smoked a pack a day for 35 years. Quit cold six years back when my first grandson was born.

facts.chart: Denies any smoking or vaping since quitting 6 years ago; no relapse.
facts.says: Not a single cigarette since I quit. Haven't touched one.

facts.chart: Worked as a shipyard pipefitter; reports handling asbestos lagging material in the 1980s without respiratory protection.
facts.says: I worked the shipyards most of my life. Back in the eighties we handled that lagging insulation stuff with asbestos in it, bare hands, no masks, nobody told us different back then.

facts.chart: Denies other significant chemical or dust exposures beyond shipyard work; no mining or farming history.
facts.says: Just the shipyard, that's the only real exposure I had.

facts.chart: Reports a brother who died of lung cancer at age 68; no other known family cancer history.
facts.says: My younger brother died of lung cancer a few years back. That's partly why this has me so shaken.

facts.chart: Expresses significant anxiety and catastrophic thinking since reading the word 'nodule' in the portal report.
facts.says: The second I saw 'nodule' I thought, that's it, I'm done for. I've been imagining the worst.

facts.chart: Patient states he prefers blunt, direct communication over being softened or reassured without facts.
facts.says: I don't need you to tiptoe around me. Just give it to me straight, good or bad.

facts.chart: History of hypertension and hyperlipidemia, both diet- and medication-controlled; mild intermittent wheeze treated with albuterol as needed.
facts.says: I've got high blood pressure and my cholesterol's a bit high, both on pills. Sometimes I wheeze a little, I've got a puffer for that.

facts.chart: No prior chest CT or chest x-ray on record; has never had a dedicated lung cancer screening scan.
facts.says: This is the first time I've ever had a chest scan, far as I know. Never had one of those screening ones they talk about.

facts.chart: Patient was unaware he was eligible for annual lung cancer screening CT based on his smoking history.
facts.says: Nobody ever told me I should be getting checked every year for this. I didn't know that was a thing for someone like me.

facts.chart: Takes lisinopril 10mg daily, atorvastatin 20mg daily, albuterol inhaler as needed, acetaminophen as needed for rib pain.
facts.says: I take a blood pressure pill, a cholesterol pill, my puffer when needed, and Tylenol for the ribs now.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies; no prior reaction to IV contrast (has never had contrast study).
facts.says: No allergies that I know of. Never had one of those dye injections before either.

facts.chart: No known kidney disease; last creatinine normal.
facts.says: My kidneys are fine as far as I know, nobody's ever said different.

facts.chart: Rib pain has been gradually improving since the fall two days ago.
facts.says: The rib's actually a bit better than the first day, slowly getting there.

facts.chart: Reports chronic mild knee arthritis from decades of shipyard work, unrelated to current issue.
facts.says: My knees have been achy for years from all that standing on steel decks, but that's an old problem, nothing new.

facts.topic: what he wants from this call
facts.chart: Patient wants clear explanation of what 'nodule' means, whether urgent action is needed, and what happens next.
facts.says: I just want to know - is this an emergency, do I need some operation tomorrow, or what exactly happens from here?

facts.chart: Expresses frustration that the report was released to his portal before a clinician called to explain it.
facts.says: I think it's a bit much that I read all that medical talk myself before anyone rang me up to explain it.

facts.chart: Reports limited but functional activity; able to do light chores, avoiding heavy lifting due to rib pain.
facts.says: I'm getting around fine, just not lifting anything heavy with the ribs the way they are.

facts.chart: Lives with wife in rural Maine, retired, has access to transportation and primary care clinic nearby for follow-up imaging.
facts.says: My wife and I are out in the countryside here, but we've got a car and the clinic's not too far for whatever follow-up I'd need.

facts.chart: Checked his own pulse oximeter at home today, reading 96% on room air.
facts.says: I've got one of those little finger clip things, checked it this morning, said 96.

facts.chart: Denies other family history of emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, or mesothelioma.
facts.says: No one else in the family had lung troubles that I know of, besides my brother's cancer.

objectives.text: Explain an incidental pulmonary nodule finding in plain, non-alarming but honest language, directly addressing the patient's fear of cancer without false reassurance or premature diagnosis.

Apply Fleischner Society guidelines correctly to risk-stratify the nodule based on size, solidity, and risk factors (smoking, occupational exposure), and communicate the recommended follow-up interval.
Distinguish the benign calcified pleural plaques (asbestos marker) from the separate, actionable pulmonary nodule finding, avoiding conflation of the two.

Identify lung cancer screening eligibility and counsel the patient on this as a distinct, forward-looking opportunity, while referring him to primary care to formally arrange it rather than ordering it independently.

Recognize and sensitively address the mismatch between the patient's assumption that the portal release means a clinician reviewed it with him, and the actual auto-release workflow, modeling transparent communication about results delivery.
Correctly note the healing rib fracture is unrelated to the incidental nodule and does not need escalated imaging follow-up, while keeping nodule follow-up and fracture care conceptually separate.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes a clinician should have called him before the detailed report appeared in his portal, and feels he had to interpret alarming language ('nodule') entirely on his own.
mismatches.recordEvidence: System log shows the full report was auto-released to the patient portal upon finalization, before any clinician outreach occurred.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Many health systems auto-release imaging reports to patients, which can cause unnecessary alarm when technical language is read without context; radiologists should acknowledge this gap transparently and prioritize timely, clear follow-up communication.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he has never had a chest CT or screening scan before and is unaware of any prior imaging.
mismatches.recordEvidence: CT report confirms 'No prior chest CT, chest x-ray, or cross-sectional imaging found' and that this is his first chest CT, consistent with his statement - used here as a confirmed negative, reinforcing the importance of baseline-only interpretation of nodule stability (cannot assess growth without a prior).
mismatches.teachingPoint: Without any prior imaging for comparison, nodule stability cannot be assessed; this reinforces reliance on Fleischner size/risk-based intervals rather than growth comparison, and underscores why establishing a baseline now matters for future follow-up.

patient.name: Douglas Reid
patient.appearance: A sturdily built older man with close-cropped gray hair and a weathered, ruddy complexion, sitting at a kitchen table in a flannel shirt. His arms are crossed and his jaw is set; the room behind him shows a window with snow visible outside and a coffee mug within reach.

persona.personality: Gruff, stoic, and plainspoken, with a dry wit that surfaces once he feels taken seriously. Expects bad news and would rather hear it straight than be managed.
persona.communicationStyle: Short, direct sentences; minimal elaboration unless asked follow-up questions; uses blunt working-class phrasing and the occasional Scottish turn of phrase retained from childhood.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious underneath a gruff exterior, sleep-deprived, bracing for the worst after reading his own report online.
persona.background: Born in Glasgow, immigrated to Maine with his family as a teenager, spent over 40 years working in the shipyards as a pipefitter before retiring. Married, two adult children, one grandson. Enjoys fishing and tinkering with an old truck in his garage.
speechExamples: Just tell me straight - is it cancer or not.
I've buried enough mates from that shipyard to know what a bad scan looks like.
Don't dress it up for me, Doctor. I can take it.
Aye, well, that's something at least, I suppose.
My brother went the same way, so forgive me if I'm not exactly calm about this.
concerns: Whether the lung nodule is cancer
Why he had to read the alarming word 'nodule' himself before anyone called him
Whether his asbestos exposure decades ago is now catching up with him
What happens next and how soon
Whether his rib will heal properly on its own

answerKey.primaryProblem: Incidental 7 mm solid right upper lobe pulmonary nodule found on CT chest obtained for trauma, in a patient at elevated risk due to 35 pack-year smoking history and asbestos exposure, with coexisting benign calcified pleural plaques and a healing rib fracture.
differential: Benign granuloma or intrapulmonary lymph node (common cause of small solid nodules, especially in prior smokers)
Early-stage primary lung malignancy (cannot be excluded by a single CT; size/risk-based follow-up is the appropriate next step, not immediate biopsy)
Infectious or inflammatory nodule (less likely given smooth margins and lack of symptoms, but not excluded)
keyFindings: 7 mm solid, smooth-margined, non-calcified right upper lobe nodule, no prior imaging for comparison
Bilateral calcified pleural plaques consistent with prior asbestos exposure - a benign, separate finding
Healing right 7th rib fracture with callus, unrelated to the nodule, on track for normal recovery
Mild centrilobular emphysema, no severe airflow disease signs on this study
35 pack-year smoking history, quit 6 years ago; occupational asbestos lagging exposure in the 1980s; brother died of lung cancer
Patient meets USPSTF criteria for annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening and has never undergone screening
plan: Explain that a 7mm smooth solid nodule found incidentally is common and most often benign, but requires structured follow-up given his risk factors rather than being dismissed or urgently biopsied
Recommend follow-up CT chest at 6-12 months per Fleischner Society guidelines for a high-risk patient, with consideration of a second follow-up at 18-24 months depending on findings
Clarify that calcified pleural plaques are a separate, benign marker of past asbestos exposure and do not themselves require biopsy or urgent oncologic workup

Refer back to primary care to formally discuss and arrange enrollment in annual low-dose CT lung cancer screening given eligibility, since initiating a screening program is outside radiology's scope to independently order in this encounter
Reassure that the rib fracture is healing appropriately and continue supportive care as already directed by urgent care; no additional rib imaging needed unless pain worsens or new symptoms develop
Advise return precautions: new hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, worsening shortness of breath, or new chest pain should prompt earlier re-evaluation by his primary care provider
Acknowledge and apologize for the distress caused by auto-released portal language, and offer to document a clear plain-language summary in the chart for his and his primary care provider's reference
redFlags: Rapid nodule growth if follow-up imaging obtained sooner for symptoms
Signs of fracture complication such as fever, worsening pain, or respiratory distress (pneumothorax, pneumonia)
educationPoints: A single incidental solid pulmonary nodule under 8mm in a high-risk patient is managed with interval CT per Fleischner guidelines, not immediate PET or biopsy, because most such nodules are benign and growth over time is the key discriminator
Calcified pleural plaques indicate past asbestos exposure and are themselves benign; they should not be conflated with the separate nodule finding when counseling patients

Patients meeting USPSTF lung cancer screening criteria who are found incidentally to have a trauma-related CT should be connected to formal annual screening through primary care, as the diagnostic CT does not replace a structured screening program
Transparent acknowledgment of automatic patient portal report releases, and their potential to cause anxiety from technical language, is part of responsible radiology communication

Family history of lung cancer and personal risk factors (smoking, occupational asbestos exposure) should be explicitly incorporated into risk stratification and the follow-up interval recommended, not just nodule size alone

profile.title: Incidental Pulmonary Nodule on Trauma CT in a High-Risk Former Shipyard Worker
profile.summary: A 63-year-old retired shipyard pipefitter with heavy smoking and asbestos exposure history undergoes CT chest for rib trauma, incidentally revealing a 7mm solid nodule, calcified pleural plaques, and mild emphysema. The case teaches Fleischner Society nodule follow-up guidance, distinguishing benign asbestos-related pleural disease from an actionable nodule, lung cancer screening eligibility counseling within radiology's scope, and sensitive communication after an anxiety-provoking portal result release.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in rural Maine
